title: Attention, always
hook: once you relax your attention, don't think you can pick it back up whenever you like

segments.voice: Yesterday: ataraxia, peace of mind, the pond unstirred under the noise. Did something noisy try to stir you, and did you stay underneath? Day four hundred twenty-nine.

You pick up your phone to check one thing, the weather. Twenty minutes later you're watching a stranger restore a rusted frying pan, and you have no memory of deciding to. You never checked the weather. Everyone knows this slide. Epictetus knew it too, without the phone. Near the end of the Discourses, book four, chapter twelve, there's a short, sharp talk about exactly this: what happens when you let your attention go, and why getting it back is harder than it looks. Today: attention, always.
screen: `CHECK THE WEATHER.` → `TWENTY MINUTES LATER: A FRYING PAN.` → `ATTENTION, ALWAYS.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Prosochē is Greek for attention, from a verb that means to hold toward: to hold the mind toward something. For Epictetus it's the watchfulness under every other practice. You can't sort what's yours from what isn't if you aren't paying attention when the moment arrives. Second, the warning. He says: when you relax your attention for a little while, don't imagine you can pick it back up whenever you like. Today's slip makes tomorrow's slip easier. A habit of not attending forms quietly, and then you're always putting it off. Tomorrow I'll be careful, people say. Which means, he points out, that today you won't be. Third, the craftsman. Nothing gets done well, he says, without attention. Not by the carpenter, not by the person steering a ship. Why would living well be the one craft you could do half asleep? Fourth, the honest part. Can anyone be faultless? No, Epictetus says plainly. That isn't possible. What is possible is to keep straining toward not making mistakes. And if, by never letting attention go completely, we avoid even a few faults, that's worth having. He isn't asking for perfection. He's asking you to keep showing up to your own life. Later, the desert monks of early Christianity made prosochē one of their own words for watchfulness of the heart. The same small word, carried down a different road. Attention isn't something you finish. It's something you return to, and the returning is the practice.
screen: `PROSOCHĒ: HOLDING THE MIND TOWARD.` · `A SLIP TODAY MAKES TOMORROW'S EASIER.` · `NO CRAFT IS DONE HALF ASLEEP.` · `NOT FAULTLESS: ALWAYS RETURNING.` · then, large: `ATTENTION.`

segments.voice: Choose one small task you can do right now: folding a shirt, washing a cup, writing one sentence, or simply breathing. For the next two minutes, give it all of you. Feel the fabric, the water, the pen. When your mind wanders, and it will, notice where it went and bring it back, gently, without scolding. That return is the whole exercise. Count your returns if you like. Each one is a rep. The bell holds the time.
Prosochē. Greek for attention, holding the mind toward what's in front of you; for Epictetus, the watchfulness every other practice depends on. Today's word.
Your line: attention. Pick one task today and attend to it fully, start to finish. When you drift, don't wait for tomorrow. Come back now. Day four hundred twenty-nine.

howItsDone: Stoic practice includes prosochē, a steady watchfulness over one's own judgments and actions, renewed many times a day whenever attention slips.

original.note: Greek: attention, from prosechein, to hold the mind toward; a core Stoic practice.

trapdoor: what you thought: attention means focusing hard for a test.
what it means: for Epictetus, prosochē is a constant watchfulness you return to again and again, not something you finish.
what a scholar hears: prosochē passed from the Stoics into early Christian monastic writing, where it named watchfulness over one's thoughts.

notes: Discourses 4.12 (On attention): relaxing attention, 'tomorrow I will attend', the craftsman and helmsman, faultlessness impossible but constant striving possible; paraphrased. Long's wording begins approximately 'When you have remitted your attention for a short time'; left unquoted.
Prosochē from prosechein (ton noun), 'to hold the mind toward': standard; confirm.
Prosochē in early Christian monastic writing (e.g. the Philokalia, desert tradition): mentioned briefly as a neighbor; confirm phrasing.
